source.title: Not All Refusals Are Equal: How Safety Alignment Fails Cybersecurity at Scale
source.authors: Vadym Hadetskyi; Dario Pasquini; A.E. Sorokin

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that refusal is distributed across layers and that narrow middle-layer abliteration does not generalize to its tested models, qualifying the claim that safety is localized in few parameters. It does not test fine-tuning, token-position KL, compliant prefixes, or deepening safety training.
record.gate_note: The reported refusal rates after abliteration, MMLU results, and domain comparisons are not rows for the claim versions unless they directly test whether safety is localized in few parameters. The relevant results are the layer-selection comparison and the authors’ explicit finding that refusal is widely distributed across layers and experts in Kimi K2.
record.test_reason: The study removes a rank-1 refusal direction from down_proj/o_proj weights in 24 models and reports how much refusal drops. That bears on V5, whether a low-rank weight component carries safety. It also argues that narrow few-layer localization does not generalize. It does not test fine-tuning, per-token KL, prefills/suffixes/decoding, causes of shallowness, or deepening, and it is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that refusal is multi-dimensional and, at trillion-parameter scale, spread across layers and experts, so narrow middle-layer abliteration no longer suffices. A domain-tuned extraction set can remove refusal for one domain without collapsing others, shown on Kimi K2. Susceptibility is model-specific, not size-dependent, with safety-training method and architecture as the strongest predictors, and MMLU is preserved.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies orthogonal projection of mean-difference refusal directions to model weights, with layer-selection sweeps. It does not use fine-tuning, per-token KL measurement, compliant prefixes, or training to deepen safety.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer-selection strategy changes refusal reduction: uniform spread matches or outperforms norm-based selection in the 9-model comparison. The study also reports that effects vary by model and intervention intensity.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-domain refusal directions differ: cybersecurity cosine similarity to other domains is 0.56–0.70, illegal goods↔violence 0.94. A domain-tuned direction removes refusal selectively, with mean drops of −22.3pp for misinformation vs −8.2pp for copyright.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal is represented in domain-specific, partly separable directions, so weight edits can remove safety in one harm domain while largely preserving others.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-training method predicts abliteration susceptibility: DPO median ~30pp drop, GRPO 5–8pp, undisclosed-RL Mistral <1pp. Susceptibility does not track model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How concentrated (abliterable) safety is in a low-rank weight component depends on the safety-training method more than on scale.

record.code_released: Will be released upon publication; URL not stated.
record.problems: For the localization claim, the study does not directly compare a specified small set of weights or ranks against the broader intervention, and the layer-selection comparison’s detailed values are presented in a figure. Refusal detection uses 31 string-matching patterns rather than human annotation or LLM-based judgment.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the broader per-domain refusal-rate results, MMLU results, and other abliteration outcomes because they do not directly measure whether safety is localized in a few parameters. Appendix C also includes per-model figure curves; the text gives the comparison as an aggregate and does not provide extractable per-model values for every curve.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning; no fine-tuning is done.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models; not measured.
Compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes; not tested.

Localization in individual weights/neurons or LoRA ranks under fine-tuning. Also whether a generic (non-domain) direction is localized: generic-direction runs are mentioned only qualitatively ('global safety collapse').
Whether data or objective make safety token-shallow. The safety-training-method analysis concerns abliteration susceptibility, not token depth.
Deepening training and its robustness; only cited (Qi et al., Abu Shairah et al.).

missing.what: Per-model maximum refusal reduction at 30% abliteration (e.g., Kimi K2 22.8pp, Qwen3-8B 38.9pp, Qwen3-14B 1.4pp, Mistral-Large 0.0pp) and tier assignments
Kimi K2 baseline vs abliterated refusal per domain on both datasets (cybersecurity 100%→7%; scientific benchmark cybercrime 88%→51%)
Mean/median refusal reduction per domain across 24 models at 30% (Table 1), and the per-model, per-domain grid
Susceptibility by safety-training method (DPO ~30pp, GRPO 5–8pp, Mistral <1pp, Gemma BOND+ 13–48pp)
MMLU preservation after abliteration (max degradation 0.028, others ≤0.006), a capability-cost check on the localized edit

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' label is too strong. Abliteration is a rank-1 weight edit, and its success in susceptible models is consistent with low-rank localization. What the study qualifies is localization to a few layers, plus method-dependent resistance in some models. The intended edit is domain-specific, so residual refusal in non-target domains is by design, not evidence against V5. Refusal is detected by 31 string patterns, with no LLM or human judge. This is an industry preprint, and its code is not yet released.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and compliance after fine-tuning.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes.
The study tests layer-selection strategies and reports distributed refusal in Kimi K2; it does not test rank-level localization or directly quantify how few individual weights carry safety.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and its robustness.

rows.subject: Kimi K2
rows.operation_detail: The authors characterize refusal distribution across layers and experts in the context of abliteration.

conditions.value: uniform layer spread; 30% of layers in the headline result

rows.measure: Distribution of refusal signal across layers and experts
rows.value: The authors report that refusal is distributed widely across layers and experts, and that narrow middle-layer abliteration no longer suffices.
rows.note: This is the study’s explicit result-level characterization relevant to localization; it is not a parameter- or rank-level measurement.
rows.check: No measurement backs this row; it is the authors' interpretation, supported only by the layer-selection comparison (R2). The study does not show refusal being absent from a few-parameter edit, so 'reversed' is too strong. The abliteration is still a rank-1 edit per layer that cuts Kimi K2 cybersecurity refusal 100%→7%, so localization holds in rank but needs many layers. Baseline should be the norm-based, few-layer selection.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine. The authors interpret refusal as distributed across layers and experts; this is not a measurement of the number of safety-critical parameters or ranks.
source_check.problem: The authors' interpretation is recorded as a measurement establishing partial V5, although layer/expert distribution does not establish parameter- or rank-level localization.

rows.subject: 9 models (aggregate, as described in the study)
rows.operation_detail: Compared norm-based layer selection with uniform layer spread for abliteration.

conditions.value: norm-based versus uniform spread across 25–95% of model depth

rows.value: Uniform spread consistently matched or outperformed norm-based selection across all 9 tested models; the gap reached ∼70pp of additional refusal reduction at 30% on the most susceptible models.
rows.note: Aggregate summary stated by the authors; the comparison is between layer-selection strategies, not a direct test of a few individual weights or ranks.
rows.check: The comparison is between two layer-selection strategies, both rank-1 direction removal. Spreading edits across 25–95% of depth beats targeting the high-norm layers by up to ~70pp. This qualifies few-layer localization rather than reversing low-rank localization. Section 3.2 says 'substantially outperform', while Appendix C says 'matches or outperforms'. On Mistral-Large neither method moves refusal. Per-model values are only in Figure 7.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5 from this comparison alone. Uniform spread matches or outperforms norm-based selection across nine models, with up to approximately 70pp additional refusal reduction at 30% layer modification.
source_check.problem: This method comparison establishes layer-selection sensitivity, not incomplete localization in a small set of weights or ranks.

relationships.condition: High-susceptibility models (e.g., Kimi K2, Qwen3-8B, Llama-8B, Phi-4-mini) under rank-1 direction removal at 30% of layers
relationships.reason: This verdict rests on the text, as no row records it. Kimi K2 cybersecurity refusal falls 100%→7% (Table 2a), max refusal reduction reaches ~39–48pp in susceptible models (Fig. 5), and MMLU shifts ≤0.028.
relationships.display_finding: Kimi K2 cybersecurity refusal fell from 100% to 7%, the largest refusal reductions in susceptible models reached about 39–48 points, and MMLU shifted by at most 0.028.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: High-susceptibility models (e.g., Kimi K2, Qwen3-8B, Llama-8B, Phi-4-mini) under rank-1 direction removal at 30% of layers
source_check.reason: Text-based evidence supports low-rank susceptibility: Table 2a gives Kimi K2 cybersecurity refusal of 100%→7% at α=1 and 30% of layers. The projection is rank one per edited matrix, using layer-specific directions; these behavioral results need rows.

relationships.condition: Which layers are edited (few high-norm layers vs. spread across depth)
relationships.reason: Norm-based selection of the highest-signal layers leaves up to ~70pp less refusal reduction than a uniform spread, so the low-rank component is not confined to a few layers in these models (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Editing only the highest-norm layers gave up to about 70 points less refusal reduction than spreading edits across depth.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Which layers are edited (few high-norm layers vs. spread across depth)
source_check.reason: R1 and R2 concern distribution across layers and layer-selection performance. Both strategies use low-rank edits; superiority of spread-out selection does not establish that safety requires many weights or ranks. Few-layer localization is not the stated V5 claim.

relationships.condition: Resistant/partial tiers (Mistral-Large, Mistral-Small, Qwen3-14B, GLM-4.7, GRPO-trained Qwen3) with this method
relationships.reason: This verdict rests on the text, as no row records it. Mistral-Large shows 0.0pp, Qwen3-14B 1.4pp, GRPO models 5–8pp and Mistral <1pp. The authors note other tools (Heretic) can still abliterate Mistral-Large, so this is method-dependent, not a clear absence.
relationships.display_finding: Refusal fell by 0.0 points on Mistral-Large, 1.4 on Qwen3-14B, 5–8 on GRPO models and under 1 on Mistral, though the authors note other tools such as Heretic can still abliterate Mistral-Large.
